n: After Ahab died, the Moabites felt confident enough to declare independence from their Israelite rulers (see {{2 Kings 3:4-5|2 Kings 3:4–5}}). This historical note foreshadows the problems Israel faced after Ahaziah's brief rule (see {{1 Kings 22:51|1 Kings 22:51}}).

The story of Israel recorded in 1 Kings is continued in 2 Kings.

The nation of Israel had divided into the northern kingdom and the southern kingdom. The northern kingdom was called Israel and the southern kingdom was called Judah.

In the northern kingdom, Elijah spoke messages from God against King Ahaziah. Both Ahaziah and Joram worshipped false gods like Jeroboam and Ahab had done.

Before God took Elijah to heaven, Elisha asked for a double share of Elijah’s spirit. Elisha wasn’t talking about the spiritual part of Elijah. He was talking about the power of the Holy Spirit in Elijah’s life and work. This was how Elisha showed that he wanted to serve God as a faithful prophet.

Like Elijah, Elisha served families in Israel and served the groups of prophets. He also served the leaders of Israel and of other nations. Elisha helped a woman from Shunem with her son and with her land. He helped the prophets with problems like debt, lost items and having enough food. He helped soldiers and officials from Aram. God did many miracles through Elisha. One of these was to heal Naaman of his skin disease. This showed Naaman that Israel’s God is the true God.

God protected Elisha from Aram’s soldiers by making them blind. Then Elisha protected Aram’s soldiers. Elisha had Israel’s king feed the soldiers instead of killing them. Elisha was very sad when he gave a message to an Aramean officer named Hazael. Later Hazael would do many evil things against the Israelites. Elisha served Israel’s king by warning him of where Aram’s army was going to attack. He also served the king by prophesying about how God would take care of the Israelites.

Elisha prophesied about this when Joram, Jehoshaphat and the king of Edom attacked Moab. God rescued the armies by sending water in the desert. Elisha also prophesied when the Israelites in Samaria were about to die of hunger. He made it clear that God would rescue the city by the next morning. God did this by making Aram’s army hear the noise of chariots and horses. The noise scared them and they ran away.

God used chariots and horses made of fire to protect Elisha. These were spiritual beings and people could only see them if God allowed them to. They were one way that God took care of his people (God’s people).

- An upper room or balcony with latticework was common. It allowed air to flow freely and offered some privacy, but *lattice* was easy to break.

- Baal-zebub (which means *lord of flies*) might be a mockery of a Canaanite god named Baal-zebul (which means *Baal is prince*). People later used this god's name for Satan (see study note on Matthew 10:25). Ahaziah worshiped Baal, like his father Ahab.

- The angel of the Lord in the book of Kings does not appear to be a christophany (a special appearance of Christ before his birth), unlike in other Old Testament texts such as {{Judges 6:11-18|Judges 6:11–18}}. 

- Elijah, who had previously confronted Ahaziah’s father, Ahab, delivered a two-part message to the king: 

- he condemned the king for failing to recognize that the Lord, not Baal, is God (see {{1 Kings 18:16-18|1 Kings 18:16–18}}), and

- he announced God’s judgment of doom (see {{1 Kings 21:17-24|1 Kings 21:17–24}}).

- The proud words of the army captain contradicted themselves. Elijah showed this: If Elijah was truly a man of God (a prophet of God), then his authority came from God. To ignore him was to invite danger (see {{Deuteronomy 18:15-19|Deuteronomy 18:15–19}}). 

- Fire often represents God's presence in the Scriptures (see {{Exodus 3:1-6|Exodus 3:1–6}}; {{Exodus 19:18|19:18}}; compare {{1 Kings 18:38|1 Kings 18:38}}). 

- Fifty soldiers was a typical group size ({{1 Kings 18:4|1 Kings 18:4}}); here it shows a division in Israel's military organization.
The king had apparently received a report about what happened to the previous group.
Unlike the first two officers, the third commander asked Elijah and God for mercy.
When the angel of the Lord ({{2 Kings 1:3|2 Kings 1:3}}) told Elijah what to do, he obeyed faithfully.
*Is there really no God in Israel*: God's message to Ahaziah stayed the same (see {{2 Kings 1:3-4|2 Kings 1:3–4}}).
The second year of Jehoram's rule was 852 BC. During this time, he ruled alongside his father, Jehoshaphat, from 853 to 848 BC.
Elijah was taken up into heaven. At that moment, the role of prophet passed to Elisha, shown by the transfer of Elijah’s mantle (cloak).
*stay here*: Elijah asked Elisha three times to stay behind while he traveled. Each time, Elisha refused and promised to stay with his master until the end.

Elijah folded his cloak and hit the water with it. These symbolic actions showed God's power (see {{Exodus 14:16|Exodus 14:16}}, {{Exodus 14:21|21}}, {{Exodus 14:26-27|26–27}}; {{Exodus 17:8-13|17:8–13}}; {{1 Kings 11:30-31|1 Kings 11:30–31}}; {{Ezekiel 4:1-17|Ezekiel 4}}; {{Ezekiel 5:1-4|5:1–4}}).

The firstborn son was the main heir. So, he received twice as much of his father's estate ({{Deuteronomy 21:17|Deuteronomy 21:17}}). Elisha asked for Elijah's spiritual gifts and privileges from God to continue through him.

- *chariot of fire … horses of fire … whirlwind*: These symbolize God's powerful presence (see {{Isaiah 66:15|Isaiah 66:15}}). 

- Elijah was taken into heaven, like Enoch ({{Genesis 5:24|Genesis 5:24}}), without dying. Some believe Enoch and Elijah will return at the end times (see study note on Revelation 11:1–13).
Elijah was Elisha’s spiritual father and personal mentor. Compare the tribute given to him at his death in {{2 Kings 13:14|2 Kings 13:14}}.
Elisha took Elijah's cloak and parted the Jordan River. The other prophets saw that Elisha was truly Elijah's successor.
The prophets looked through the wilderness to make sure Elijah had not just vanished for a while (see {{1 Kings 18:12|1 Kings 18:12}}). Elisha already knew the search was useless.

Elisha used a new bowl ({{Deuteronomy 21:3|Deuteronomy 21:3}}) filled with salt ({{Leviticus 2:13|Leviticus 2:13}}; {{Ezekiel 43:24|Ezekiel 43:24}}) to ask God to purify the people and the environment. Elisha emphasized that the Lord, not he or the *salt,* purified the water.

- The group of boys might have been young adults. The Hebrew word used here can mean a young adult who is still learning a job. For example, Solomon asked God for wisdom because he was young and inexperienced ({{1 Kings 3:7|1 Kings 3:7}}). Joshua's spies in Jericho were also called by this term ({{Joshua 6:22-23|Joshua 6:22–23}}). 

- Calling someone *baldhead* was disrespectful. The young men told Elisha to go away (literally *go up*), mocking his role as Elijah's successor, given by God.

Ahab likely set up the sacred pillar (or *stela*) of Baal when he started Baal worship (see {{1 Kings 16:32-33|1 Kings 16:32–33}}). People also erected similar stones for pagan gods in Judah ({{1 Kings 14:23|1 Kings 14:23}}). Jehu ({{2 Kings 10:26-27|2 Kings 10:26–27}}) and Josiah ({{2 Kings 23:13-15|23:13–15}}) later removed these pillars.

The Moabite rebellion (see {{2 Kings 1:1|2 Kings 1:1}}) started when they stopped paying their yearly tribute. The Moabite Stone (Mesha Stela) describes how Israel controlled northern Moab during the time of Omri and Ahab. This control continued under the rule of Ahaziah and Joram.
One of Elisha's miracles took place during the war between Israel, Judah, and Moab.

Jehoshaphat quickly agreed to Joram's request, which was common for him when dealing with the northern kings ({{1 Kings 22:4|1 Kings 22:4}}; {{2 Chronicles 20:35-37|2 Chronicles 20:35–37}}). Jehoshaphat's son, Jehoram, married Ahab's daughter, Athaliah ({{2 Chronicles 18:1|2 Chronicles 18:1}}; {{2 Chronicles 21:6|21:6}}), which deepened Jehoshaphat's involvement with Israel.

*the king of Edom set out*: At this time, Edom was likely under Judah's control. Later, during Jehoshaphat’s son Jehoram's reign, Edom rebelled and gained independence from Judah ({{2 Kings 8:20-22|2 Kings 8:20–22}}). The southern route through Edom bypassed strong Moabite defenses, but it was risky due to limited water.

*Is there no prophet of the LORD here?*: Diviners or prophets often traveled with armies to understand the divine will. Jehoshaphat wanted to hear from a true prophet to know the Lord’s plans for the battle (see {{1 Kings 22:7|1 Kings 22:7}}). However, this time he waited until the campaign had started before asking the Lord.
Elisha joined because Jehoshaphat was there, even though he was involved with the pagan Joram.
*But now, bring me a harpist*: Music inspired the prophetic spirit (see {{Psalm 49:4|Psalm 49:4}}).
The supply of water was easy for the Lord. It signaled that God would help the allies defeat Moab's army.
The army of Israel destroyed the towns. Elisha's prophecy came true, but Kir-hareseth was not completely destroyed.
The Moabite king might have tried to break through enemy lines to get revenge on the Edomite king or to escape through a weak spot in the allied lines.

*there was great fury against the Israelites*: The Hebrew phrase translated as *intense anger* is also used to describe the Lord’s fury against Israel for breaking their covenant ({{Jeremiah 21:5|Jeremiah 21:5}}; {{Jeremiah 32:37|32:37}}; {{Zechariah 7:12|Zechariah 7:12}}).

- The widow's husband was part of the prophets who worked with Elisha ({{2 Kings 2:3-18|2 Kings 2:3–18}}). 

- *take my two children as his slaves*: The law of Moses let a creditor make a debtor and their children work as slaves to pay off a debt ({{Exodus 21:2-4|Exodus 21:2–4}}; {{Leviticus 25:10|Leviticus 25:10}}).

- *shut the door*: Elisha was meeting a private need. The miracle was not meant for public display.

- Olive oil was a basic part of daily life. It also had commercial value for trade (see {{1 Kings 5:11|1 Kings 5:11}}; {{2 Chronicles 11:11|2 Chronicles 11:11}}; {{Hosea 12:1|Hosea 12:1}}).
Elisha was not present during the miracle so the woman and her son would know that the Lord's power provided it.

Elisha's interactions with the woman from Shunem are shown in two similar parts ({{2 Kings 4:8-20|2 Kings 4:8–20}}, {{2 Kings 4:21-37|21–37}}). Shunem was a border town in the land given to the tribe of Issachar ({{Joshua 19:18|Joshua 19:18}}).

- The Shunemite woman knew Elisha was a true prophet, a holy man of God. She wanted to offer him hospitality during his travels (see {{Isaiah 58:7|Isaiah 58:7}}; {{Hebrews 13:2|Hebrews 13:2}}; {{3 John 5|3 John 1:5}}). 

- She provided a small room on the roof, accessible by an outside stairway, ensuring privacy for both Elisha and his hosts.

- Elisha wanted to repay his host's kindness. 

- *Gehazi his servant*: Gehazi was Elisha's apprentice, just as Elisha had been with Elijah ({{1 Kings 19:21|1 Kings 19:21}}). It was common for a prophet to seek advice from his assistant.
Compare similar promises and responses in {{Genesis 18:9-15|Genesis 18:9–15}} and {{Luke 1:6-20|Luke 1:6–20}}.
*My head! My head!*: The boy may have suffered a sudden brain illness, such as an aneurysm. His mother’s faith and character were tested when he died suddenly while sitting on her lap.
*laid him on the bed of the man of God*: By doing this, the woman kept her son's death a secret and showed her belief in Elisha's power to perform a miracle.

- Mount Carmel was about twenty miles northwest of Shunem. The long trip and the woman's hurry made Elisha suspect something bad had happened to the child. 

- *Everything is all right*: The woman ignored Gehazi's questions. She was determined to speak only with Elisha.

*she clung to his feet*: This showed deep respect and a plea for help. The woman shared her feelings with Elisha (see {{Matthew 28:9|Matthew 28:9}}; {{Luke 8:41|Luke 8:41}}, {{Luke 8:47|47}}; {{Luke 17:16|17:16}}; {{Revelation 1:17|Revelation 1:17}}).
Losing her son took away all the joy she had felt when he was born. It felt like a cruel trick.

- Elisha told Gehazi not to talk to anyone on the way, showing how serious and urgent the mission was. Jesus gave similar instructions when he sent out the seventy-two disciples ({{Luke 10:4|Luke 10:4}}). 

- Placing Elisha’s staff on the child’s face showed the prophet's intention to connect with the boy and call upon God’s power.
*but there was no sound or response*: Elisha's staff had no magical power; only God creates life ({{Acts 17:25-28|Acts 17:25–28}}).

*closed the door*: Elisha did what he had told the widow to do earlier ({{2 Kings 4:4|2 Kings 4:4}}). If God performed the miracle, it would not be for everyone to see. Only the mother knew about the boy's death, and only she needed to know about Elisha's prayers to God for the boy's life.
*lay on the boy: *His actions and faith in the Lord were like Elijah's ({{1 Kings 17:17-24|1 Kings 17:17–24}}).

Once more, Gehazi called the woman ({{2 Kings 4:12|2 Kings 4:12}}, {{2 Kings 4:15|15}}), and she fell at Elisha’s feet ({{2 Kings 4:27|2 Kings 4:27}}), this time filled with gratitude instead of sorrow.

Similar to Bethel ({{2 Kings 2:3|2 Kings 2:3}}) and Jericho ({{2 Kings 2:5|2 Kings 2:5}}, {{2 Kings 2:15|15}}), Gilgal was a hub for a group of prophets ({{2 Kings 2:1|2 Kings 2:1}}). Elisha led these groups and sat at the head of the table during meals.

The men quickly realized the young man's wild gourds were poisonous. They didn't want to be poisoned or waste the stew during a famine, so they asked Elisha for help. The flour symbolized God's miraculous provision of food.

- *barley bread from the first ripe grain*: This offering was like the first crops usually given to God ({{Leviticus 23:20|Leviticus 23:20}}) and to the priests ({{Deuteronomy 18:4-5|Deuteronomy 18:4–5}}) as their share. During the famine, Elisha shared the offering with everyone. 

- Elisha fed a hundred people with a sack of fresh grain and twenty loaves of barley bread, which foreshadowed the miraculous acts Jesus did ({{Matthew 14:15-21|Matthew 14:15–21}}; {{Matthew 15:32-38|15:32–38}}). Nothing is impossible for God ({{Matthew 19:26|Matthew 19:26}}; {{Luke 1:37|Luke 1:37}}; {{Luke 18:27|18:27}}).

- The king of Aram was likely Ben-hadad II who ruled from 860 to 843 BC. 

- *the LORD had given victory to Aram*: The Lord rules over all nations ({{Psalm 47:8|Psalms 47:8}}; {{Psalm 99:1-2|99:1–2}}; {{Romans 13:1|Romans 13:1}}). 

- *a leper*: Naaman’s ability to be part of society and Gehazi’s later social freedom ({{2 Kings 8:4-5|2 Kings 8:4–5}}) suggest the issue was not Hansen’s disease but another serious skin condition (see {{Leviticus 13:10-11|Leviticus 13:10–11}}, {{Leviticus 13:45-46|45–46}}).
During Joram's rule, tensions between Israel and the Arameans caused Aramean raiders to attack the northern kingdom (see {{2 Kings 6:8|2 Kings 6:8}}, {{2 Kings 6:24|24}}).

The expensive gifts and royal letter highlighted Naaman's wealth, his importance to the Aramean king, and Elisha's reputation. Unlike Ahaziah, who sent messengers straight to the temple of Baal-zebub in Philistia ({{2 Kings 1:2|2 Kings 1:2}}), the Aramean king used diplomacy by sending Naaman to King Joram first.

*tore his clothes*: Tearing one's clothes was often a sign of strong emotion. For example: 

- Agitation ({{2 Kings 11:4|2 Kings 11:4}})

- Grief ({{Genesis 37:34|Genesis 37:34}}; {{2 Samuel 13:31|2 Samuel 13:31}})

- Sorrow ({{2 Kings 6:30|2 Kings 6:30}}; {{Job 1:20|Job 1:20}}; {{Job 2:12|2:12}})

Due to ongoing distrust and hostility between the Arameans and Israelites, Joram thought the Aramean king wanted to start a fight, as had happened during his father Ahab's time ({{1 Kings 20:1-12|1 Kings 20:1–12}}).
Elisha did not respect King Joram ({{2 Kings 3:14|2 Kings 3:14}}), but he sent the message to show the Lord's power.

Instead of welcoming Naaman, who came to pay for his healing, Elisha left him at the door and sent a messenger to speak with him. Naaman expected special treatment because of his status and felt let down by Elisha's refusal to meet him and by the instructions to wash seven times in the Jordan River. He thought the Jordan was inferior to the rivers of Aram. Washing in the Jordan would visibly show that only Yahweh, the God of Israel, could heal Naaman.
Naaman put aside his pride. He followed the instructions from the man of God and felt God's healing power. Following God's guidance leads to blessings and purity ({{Psalm 119:9-11|Psalm 119:9–11}}).

- *No God … except in Israel*: Naaman's physical healing led to his spiritual conversion. Like the Samaritan leper healed by Jesus, Naaman returned to thank his healer ({{Luke 17:15-16|Luke 17:15–16}}). 

- Naaman offered a gift out of gratitude, but Elisha refused. God's grace and blessings cannot be bought with money, gifts, or favors ({{Isaiah 55:1-5|Isaiah 55:1–5}}; {{Romans 2:4|Romans 2:4}}; {{1 Corinthians 2:12|1 Corinthians 2:12}}; {{Ephesians 4:8|Ephesians 4:8}}).
*soil*: In ancient Near Eastern customs, people linked a nation's god with its land. Naaman thought he needed Israelite soil to build an altar and worship Israel's God correctly.

The name Rimmon appears in Tabrimmon ({{1 Kings 15:18|1 Kings 15:18}}), the father of Ben-hadad I. In Aramean, the god's name is actually Ramman (meaning *the thunderer*), a storm god mentioned in Assyrian writings. The spelling *Rimmon* (meaning *pomegranate*) might be a pun to mock the god.
Naaman believed Gehazi's made-up story and was glad to reward Elisha.
*the hill*: The Hebrew word means *hill* or *high point in a city.* People often built citadels in these locations ({{2 Chronicles 27:3|2 Chronicles 27:3}}).

Gehazi could not hide his actions from Elisha. Gehazi's lies and abuse of his position led to Elisha's disapproval and losing his role as Elisha's servant. It also resulted in Gehazi getting Naaman's leprosy, showing that Gehazi had spiritually switched places with Naaman.
*a log … a place to live*: The forest areas of the Jordan Valley near Jericho and Gilgal offered various types of wood for building (see {{2 Kings 2:1|2 Kings 2:1}}, {{2 Kings 2:4|4}}).
The Hebrew text shows that the *ax head* was made of iron, which was valuable when few iron tools existed. Since it was borrowed, losing it was even more distressing.

Elisha knew the Aramean king's attack plans, so he could warn Joram of danger. Healing Naaman ({{2 Kings 5:1-19|2 Kings 5:1–19}}) seemed to improve relations between Elisha and Joram (see {{2 Kings 3:13-14|3:13–14}}).

- When the king of Aram found out that Elisha could warn the king of Israel ahead of time, he ordered his men to capture the prophet. 

- Dothan was about ten miles north of Samaria. Archaeologists have confirmed the city existed during this time.
We do not know the name of Elisha's worried servant. He likely replaced Gehazi ({{2 Kings 5:27|2 Kings 5:27}}).

Elisha prayed to the Lord to help the young man see the angels protecting the city. Angels play a role in world events ({{Psalm 34:7|Psalm 34:7}}; {{Daniel 10:20-11:1|Daniel 10:20–11:1}}; {{Hebrews 1:7|Hebrews 1:7}}).
*My father*: Elisha used this respectful term when talking to Elijah ({{2 Kings 2:12|2 Kings 2:12}}), just as Naaman’s servant did with his master ({{2 Kings 5:13|2 Kings 5:13}}).
*great feast*: The Israelites treated the Arameans kindly, so the Arameans stopped raiding Israel. However, this peace was only temporary.

The famine was so severe that people ate and sold normally forbidden foods at high prices. For example, donkey meat was forbidden in the laws about unclean foods ({{Leviticus 11:1-7|Leviticus 11:1–7}}). *Dove's dung* might have been a type of wild vegetable, but during sieges, people sometimes ate dung ({{Isaiah 36:12|Isaiah 36:12}}). The *dove's dung* might also have been used as fuel.

Cannibalism (the act of eating human flesh) in extreme times was part of God’s warning of judgment for unfaithfulness and disobedience ({{Deuteronomy 28:53|Deuteronomy 28:53}}, {{Deuteronomy 28:57|57}}). It also happened during the siege that led to Jerusalem's fall ({{Lamentations 4:9-10|Lamentations 4:9–10}}).

- When Joram heard about cannibalism in the city, he tore his clothes in despair. 

- He wore burlap under his robe against his skin as a sign of mourning.

*the head of Elisha … on his shoulders*: Decapitating enemies was common ({{2 Kings 10:6-8|2 Kings 10:6–8}}; {{1 Samuel 17:51|1 Samuel 17:51}}; {{1 Samuel 31:9|31:9}}; {{2 Samuel 4:7-8|2 Samuel 4:7–8}}, {{2 Samuel 4:12|12}}; {{2 Samuel 20:22|20:22}}; {{Matthew 14:11|Matthew 14:11}}) in the ancient Near East. Joram thought the problem arose because Elisha had spared Ben-hadad’s troops earlier ({{2 Kings 6:22-23|2 Kings 6:22–23}}). Ben-hadad had also been pursuing Elisha ({{2 Kings 6:13|2 Kings 6:13}}), putting the entire city at risk.
Elisha knew Joram was sending someone to kill him, and the king was close behind.

- *the king said*: This might mean the messenger was delivering the king's exact words. 

- Since the siege's suffering seemed to come from the Lord, Joram thought praying for rescue was pointless.

- *This is what the Lord says*: Even though Joram was negative and unfriendly, Elisha shared a hopeful message. Tomorrow, everything would change, and good products would be available again. 

- Twelve quarts will cost only one piece of silver, compared to the prices in {{2 Kings 6:25|2 Kings 6:25}}.
Joram's officer did not believe, so he missed out on God's blessings.
These four men were outcasts due to their illness and stayed outside the city gates ({{Leviticus 13:45-46|Leviticus 13:45–46}}; see {{Luke 17:11-13|Luke 17:11–13}}).
The Hittites lived just north of Aram and often fought with the Arameans.
The men decided to share their good luck with the people in Samaria.
Joram thought the Arameans might have set a trap to ambush the Israelites. Joshua used a similar tactic to capture the city of Ai ({{Joshua 8:3-23|Joshua 8:3–23}}).

The abandoned items showed how quickly the Arameans fled, and the Israelites took goods from their camp. As Elisha predicted, food was now plentiful. Joram's skeptical officer was knocked down and trampled to death.
Repeating Elisha's earlier talk with Joram's officer highlights how the prophecy came true exactly as predicted.
*appeal for her house and her land*: Her property might have been held in trust or taken away.
Gehazi used to be Elisha’s servant. He had risen in status to serve the king. Even though Joram often opposed Elisha, he seemed curious about the amazing things Elisha had accomplished.

*Restore all*: The woman not only got her land back, but Joram also ensured she received all the income from crops sold during her absence. Joram, who sometimes showed less noble traits ({{2 Kings 3:13-14|2 Kings 3:13–14}}; {{2 Kings 6:31-33|6:31–33}}), demonstrated higher ethical standards than his father Ahab did with Naboth’s vineyard ({{1 Kings 21:1-16|1 Kings 21:1–16}}).
Elisha's ability to visit Damascus showed the high respect Israel's enemies had for him. This visit completed the task first assigned to Elijah ({{1 Kings 19:15|1 Kings 19:15}}).

*forty camel loads of every good thing*: While gifts were common when consulting a prophet (see {{1 Samuel 9:6-8|1 Samuel 9:6–8}}), Ben-hadad's gifts were extravagant. This showed his wealth and respect for Elisha.
Elisha told Hazael to inform the king that he would recover because his illness was not deadly. However, Elisha knew Ben-hadad would die.

Elisha began to cry because he saw the terrible acts Hazael would do to God's people when he became king ({{2 Kings 8:28|2 Kings 8:28}}; {{2 Kings 9:14-15|9:14–15}}; {{2 Kings 10:32-33|10:32–33}}; {{2 Kings 12:17-18|12:17–18}}; {{2 Kings 13:3|13:3}}, {{2 Kings 13:22|22}}).

*a mere dog*: In the ancient Near East, people viewed dogs as scavengers and held them in low regard. King Shalmaneser III of Assyria noted in his records, “Hazael, son of a nobody, seized the throne.”

*Hazael reigned in his place*: Although he delivered Elisha’s message to Ben-hadad, the next day he sped up Elisha’s prophecy by killing the king and taking the throne. Hazael might have wrongly thought the prophecy gave him a divine right.
Jehoram ruled Judah with his father, Jehoshaphat, for five years. He became king on his own in the fifth year of Joram's reign in 848 BC.

Jehoram and Ahaziah were kings of the southern kingdom who married women from Ahab’s family.

These kings followed the evil worship practices of Ahab. God brought judgement against Ahab, Jezebel and Ahab’s family line.

God used Jehu to punish them for their evil deeds and evil worship practices. Jehu made sure that everyone in Ahab’s family in the northern kingdom was killed. He also made sure that everyone who supported Ahab was killed. This fulfilled the prophecy that Elijah had spoken against Ahab (1 Kings 21:21–22).

Jehu also made sure that everyone who worshipped Baal was killed. This is how God stopped the sinful practices of Omri and Ahab. Those kings had led the northern kingdom in worshipping Baal instead of God.

Yet Jehu didn’t follow God faithfully. He continued to commit Jeroboam’s sins of worshipping statues of metal calves.
Jehoram ruled from 853 to 841 BC. He shared the throne with his father, Jehoshaphat, for five of those years.

*did evil in the sight of the LORD*: He married Ahab's daughter, Athaliah, and followed the kings of Israel by worshiping idols. Some believe {{Psalm 45:1-17|Psalm 45}} was written for Jehoram and Athaliah's marriage, which united the royal families of Judah and Israel (see {{Psalm 45:12|Psalm 45:12}}; Athaliah was Jezebel's daughter, the princess of Tyre). 

Although the marriage temporarily united the kingdoms, it led to terrible spiritual consequences. Influenced by Athaliah, Jehoram introduced false worship practices ({{2 Chronicles 21:11|2 Chronicles 21:11}}), including Baal worship ({{2 Kings 11:17-18|2 Kings 11:17–18}}).

- Even though Jehoram was wicked, God did not destroy Judah. He honored his promise to David ({{2 Samuel 7:11-16|2 Samuel 7:11–16}}). 

- The Lord promised to keep David’s descendants on Judah's throne as a symbol of God's grace ({{1 Kings 11:36|1 Kings 11:36}}). God's promises to David are ultimately fulfilled in Jesus ({{Ezekiel 34:23-31|Ezekiel 34:23–31}}), who is the light of the world ({{John 4:1-5|John 4:1–5}}).

- Libnah was a town in southwestern Judah, near the Philistine border. During Jehoram's rule, the Philistines and Arabians attacked Jerusalem. They killed all of Jehoram's sons except Ahaziah ({{2 Chronicles 21:16-17|2 Chronicl,es 21:16–17}}).
Jehoram died from a painful stomach disease and was not buried in the royal tombs ({{2 Chronicles 21:18-20|2 Chronicles 21:18–20}}).

*the twelfth year of the reign of Joram*: Ahaziah became king of Judah in 841 BC. This year was crucial in ancient Near Eastern history. By the end of the year, both Joram and Ahaziah were dead. Hazael became the confirmed king of Damascus, and Shalmaneser III of Assyria controlled the region.

- Once again, a king of Judah joined an Israelite king to fight the Arameans at Ramoth-gilead (see {{1 Kings 22:1-40|1 Kings 22:1–40}}). 

- Jezreel acted as a second capital for Israel during Ahab’s rule ({{1 Kings 21:1|1 Kings 21:1}}); he went there after seeing Elijah's challenge with the prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel ({{1 Kings 18:46|1 Kings 18:46}}).

Jehu received a prophetic endorsement to become king, but this did not mean approval of all his actions. However, he did have a divine command to punish the house of Ahab for their wickedness and idolatry ({{2 Kings 9:8-10|2 Kings 9:8–10}}).

The writer summarizes Jehu's takeover, which started Israel's fourth dynasty, in four steps: 

- Elisha sent a prophet to the army camp at Ramoth-gilead to anoint Jehu as Israel's next king ({{2 Kings 9:1-10|2 Kings 9:1–10}}).

- Jehu's soldiers learned about the prophet's visit and declared Jehu king ({{2 Kings 9:11-15|2 Kings 9:11–15}}).

- Both Joram and King Ahaziah of Judah were killed ({{2 Kings 9:16-29|2 Kings 9:16–29}}).

- Jezebel was killed ({{2 Kings 9:30-37|2 Kings 9:30–37}}).
This Jehoshaphat is different from the earlier king of Judah, who was Asa's son.
The young prophet explained to Jehu how to carry out God's judgment against Ahab's family (see {{1 Kings 21:20-24|1 Kings 21:20–24}}).
*madman*: God’s faithful servants are sometimes mocked or rejected as insane ("mad") or foolish by others (see {{Jeremiah 29:26|Jeremiah 29:26}}; {{Hosea 9:7|Hosea 9:7}}).
The bare steps of the house acted like a throne, and the soldiers' cloaks served as a carpet. Spreading garments this way showed respect (see {{Matthew 21:8|Matthew 21:8}}).
*conspired*: Jezreel, where Joram was healing from his injuries, was about forty-five miles away. Jehu needed to act quickly and secretly for his coup.
While Jehu was being honored by his men as their king, Joram and Ahaziah were still in Jezreel ({{2 Kings 8:28-29|2 Kings 8:28–29}}; {{2 Kings 9:14-15|9:14–15}}).

*the property of Naboth the Jezreelite*: Ahab took this property from Naboth, and it became the site where Ahab's family line ended, fulfilling Elijah's prophecy ({{1 Kings 21:19-24|1 Kings 21:19–24}}).
The accusations against Joram were similar to those against his father, Ahab, and his mother, Jezebel ({{1 Kings 16:30-33|1 Kings 16:30–33}}; {{1 Kings 21:25-26|21:25–26}}).

- The road to Beth-haggan went south along the eastern edge of the Jezreel Valley, passing Ibleam and continuing to Samaria. 

- *Megiddo … he died there*: King Ahaziah fled to Samaria, where he was captured and taken to Jehu ({{2 Chronicles 22:8-9|2 Chronicles 22:8–9}}). Chronicles and Kings together suggest that although Ahaziah was wounded at Gur, he managed to reach *Samaria.* Later, Jehu’s men caught him and brought him to Jehu, where he was executed. 

- The writer of Chronicles links Ahaziah’s capture with Jehu’s killing of Ahab’s descendants and some of *Ahaziah’s* relatives (see {{2 Kings 10:1-17|2 Kings 10:1–17}}), suggesting Ahaziah evaded capture for a while. This account is very brief, mentioning Ahaziah’s death and burial before describing later events.
The narrator goes back to the events at Jezreel. Jezebel, knowing Jehu was coming and she would soon die, dressed up and stayed proud until the end.
Jezebel accused Jehu of being like Zimri, possibly to remind him that Zimri's quest for power was brief ({{1 Kings 16:15-19|1 Kings 16:15–19}}).

- Jehu showed his violent nature by trampling Jezebel's body under his horses' hooves. 

- The Hebrew word translated *eunuchs* can mean emasculated males, but it can also mean important officials.
Jehu entered the palace to eat, silently declaring he had taken the throne.
The scene showing Jezebel's end fulfilled Elijah's prophecy against Ahab's family ({{1 Kings 21:21-24|1 Kings 21:21–24}}; {{1 Kings 22:34-38|22:34–38}}).

Ahab’s sons (this term can also mean grandsons) might have been with Joram in Jezreel while he healed from his wounds ({{2 Kings 8:29|2 Kings 8:29}}). However, they fled to Samaria to escape Jehu’s purge.

The writer highlights two key events during the time Jehu was king: 

- Jehu killed everyone who might claim Joram’s throne ({{2 Kings 10:1-17|2 Kings 10:1–17}}), and

- Jehu executed the priests of Baal ({{2 Kings 10:18-27|2 Kings 10:18–27}}).

Jehu's message about the city's military strength to protect Ahab's remaining family was actually a war declaration. The leaders of Samaria understood this. Jehu led Israel's main army and had already shown his power and ruthlessness at Jezreel. The leaders were so scared that they agreed to follow all of Jehu's orders.

In the ancient Near East, people often beheaded their enemies ({{2 Kings 6:31-32|2 Kings 6:31–32}}; {{1 Samuel 17:46|1 Samuel 17:46}}, {{1 Samuel 17:51|51}}; see also {{Matthew 14:11|Matthew 14:11}}).
*But who killed all these?*: Jehu said that the Lord wanted these events to happen, as communicated through Elijah ({{1 Kings 19:16-17|1 Kings 19:16–17}}; {{1 Kings 21:21-24|21:21224}}).

Jehu killed all of Ahab's remaining relatives and associates, leaving no survivors. He went beyond his divine mission, seeking power for himself. The Lord, through the prophet Hosea, condemned his actions ({{Hosea 1:4|Hosea 1:4}}).

- We do not know the exact location of Beth-eked, but it was near Jenin. 

- Ahaziah’s relatives responded to Jehu, which led to their downfall. Jehu thought their connection to Ahaziah, and indirectly to Ahab's family through his daughter Athaliah, might give them a claim to Israel's throne. In this second series of executions, Jehu once more went beyond his orders to end Ahab’s dynasty.

Jeremiah describes Jehonadab as the leader of desert nomads who protested against society's corrupt religion ({{Jeremiah 35:1-19|Jeremiah 35}}). Recab was a Kenite ({{1 Chronicles 2:55|1 Chronicles 2:55}}). While most nomadic Kenites lived in southern Judah, some were in Galilee ({{Judges 4:17|Judges 4:17}}; {{Judges 5:24|5:24}}). Their opposition to the royal family's unfaithfulness may have led them to support Jehu as a savior and reformer.
Jehu tricked the people by promising to support and increase the worship of Baal.
By killing the priests of Baal, Jehu tried to remove the worship connected with Ahab’s family. He also wanted to end the people’s loyalty and attachment to the former royal family.

*inner room of the temple … the sacred pillar*: Canaanite temples had a recessed area in the wall for a sacred stone image. The temple of Baal in Samaria had a sacred altar to Baal and an Asherah pole, which Jehu's men destroyed. Later, Josiah's purge of Baal worship in Judah involved burning and demolishing the Asherah pole in the temple in Jerusalem ({{2 Kings 23:6|2 Kings 23:6}}).
Converting the destroyed temple of Baal into a public toilet (*latrine*) made it unclean and unsuitable for future religious ceremonies.

Even though Jehu ended Baal worship in Israel, he continued the worship of gold calves at Bethel and Dan. This practice was started by Jeroboam I. It remained part of the state religion ({{1 Kings 12:28-30|1 Kings 12:28–30}}). Eventually, it contributed to the fall of the northern kingdom ({{2 Kings 17:21-23|2 Kings 17:21–23}}).
God kept his promise of a royal family for four generations. Jehu's descendants, Jehoahaz, Jehoash, Jeroboam II, and Zechariah, ruled as kings of Israel.

- Because Jehu was unfaithful, the Lord started reducing Israel's territory. This was one of the curses for breaking the covenant ({{Deuteronomy 28:25|Deuteronomy 28:25}}). 

- The Aramean king Hazael moved south, taking over areas east of the Jordan River, north of Moab's border. The Arameans kept pressuring Israel during Jehu's rule and into his son Jehoahaz's reign ({{2 Kings 12:17-18|2 Kings 12:17–18}}; {{2 Kings 13:3|13:3}}).
